title: Five Indian Seafarers Rescued After Projectile Strikes Kuwait-Flagged Tanker in Strait of Hormuz
excerpt: The Indian Embassy in Oman coordinated the rescue of the five crew members aboard MT Kazimah III and brought them safely ashore, amid heightened monitoring of thousands of Indian seafarers in the region.
body:
• Five Indian nationals aboard the Kuwait-flagged crude oil tanker MT Kazimah III were rescued and brought ashore after the vessel was struck by a projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz.
  • The Embassy of India in Oman said it coordinated the rescue operation on Friday and thanked Omani authorities for their support; all five seafarers are safe.
  • The tanker was en route to the port of Lomé in Togo when it was hit; shipping data identifies it as a crude carrier sailing under the Kuwaiti flag.
  • The rescue comes amid heightened monitoring of Indian seafarers in the region: the External Affairs Ministry says more than 4,500 Indian crew are aboard commercial vessels operating in and around the Gulf.

Five Indian nationals aboard the Kuwait-flagged crude oil tanker MT Kazimah III were rescued and brought ashore after the vessel was struck by a projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, the Embassy of India in Oman said.

In a statement posted on social media on Friday, the Indian mission in Muscat said it had coordinated the rescue of the five crew members after the tanker was hit in the strategically vital waterway. "All 5 Indian nationals have been shifted ashore safely," the embassy said, thanking Omani authorities for their continued support and assistance during the operation.

Context & Background

The MT Kazimah III is a crude oil tanker sailing under the Kuwaiti flag that was en route to the port of Lomé in Togo when the incident occurred, according to shipping data and Indian officials. The Strait of Hormuz, connecting the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea, is the world's most consequential energy chokepoint — roughly a fifth of global petroleum liquids consumption passes through it.

https://x.com/EconomicTimes/status/2106265828702179661

The attack is the second projectile strike in recent weeks to ensnare Indian seafarers near Oman. Last month's attack on the MV Cape Dao killed one Indian crew member, underscoring the growing danger to civilian mariners as commercial vessels face escalating attacks amid regional tensions. External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar raised the issue at the 81st UN General Assembly last week, noting Indian seafarers had lost their lives in such attacks and announcing that India had joined Liberia and 23 partner nations to build international support for protecting commercial shipping routes. India has responded by tightening its watch over its maritime workforce: External Affairs Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said on Tuesday that more than 4,500 Indian seafarers were aboard commercial vessels operating in the region, including 163 Indian crew on 12 active cargo ships — six India-flagged vessels and six foreign-flagged vessels carrying cargo to India.

"We remain committed to the safety, security and welfare of our seafarers abroad."

— Ministry of External Affairs, confirming the rescue

Impact & Analysis

The strike deepens the security questions hanging over one of the world's busiest shipping lanes. For tanker owners and insurers, projectile attacks in the Hormuz corridor raise war-risk premiums and route-planning costs that eventually feed into freight rates. For India, which depends on the Gulf for crude imports and employs tens of thousands of seafarers on foreign-flagged vessels, each incident tests the reach of its consular and maritime response network — the Muscat mission's rapid coordination this time offered a clean contrast to incidents that end in fatalities.

The Ministry of Shipping, working with Indian diplomatic missions and local authorities, continues to monitor vessel movements in the region, Jaiswal said, adding that missions and stakeholders would provide assistance wherever required.

Diaspora Angle

For the families of the estimated 4,500-plus Indian seafarers working commercial vessels in and around the Gulf, this week's news cuts close. Indian crew are among the largest national contingents in global merchant shipping, and the Hormuz incident is a reminder of the physical risk that underwrites that workforce's remittance economy. The External Affairs Ministry says concerned families can seek help through the relevant Indian mission in the region.

What's Next

The immediate questions are who launched the projectile and whether further attacks on commercial traffic will follow — neither had been publicly established at the time of writing. India will keep its monitoring posture in place, and the rescued crew are now ashore in Oman. What bears watching is whether insurers and ship operators begin rerouting or repricing Hormuz transits — the point at which security incidents in the strait start showing up in energy prices.
